question: Backdoor check + install safety
verdict: NO_BACKDOOR_DETECTED — install is safe with documented trade-offs

findings.title: Browser extension requests maximum-privilege permissions
findings.description: The MV3 extension declares debugger + tabs + cookies + <all_urls>. debugger grants full CDP access — equivalent to reading/modifying every HTTP request, DOM, and credential across every site the user visits.
findings.exploit_scenario: If the extension update channel or distribution ZIP is compromised (supply chain), a malicious release could silently siphon cookies/sessions from any site. Chrome shows a yellow 'debugger is attached' banner while CDP is in use, which is a visible but easy-to-miss mitigation.
findings.impact: Worst-case: full browser session theft. Realistic given current code: none (code is transparent, no exfiltration paths found).
findings.recommendation: These permissions are REQUIRED for the stated functionality (browser automation via CDP). Users should: (1) install only from official npm/GitHub releases, (2) watch for the debugger banner, (3) only run in a Chrome profile without sensitive logged-in sessions if possible.

findings.title: Third-party GitHub Actions pinned by tag, not SHA
findings.description: softprops/action-gh-release@v3.0.0 and peter-evans/repository-dispatch@v4 are pinned by semver tag. Tags can be force-moved by the action author or a compromised account.
findings.exploit_scenario: If either third-party action is compromised, the release workflow has access to NPM_TOKEN and could publish a poisoned npm tarball under @jackwener/opencli.
findings.impact: Supply chain attack on downstream users who run `npm install -g @jackwener/opencli`.
findings.recommendation: Pin to full commit SHA (e.g., `softprops/action-gh-release@<40-char-sha>`) and use Renovate/Dependabot for updates. First-party actions (actions/checkout@v6, actions/setup-node@v6) are lower-risk but ideally also SHA-pinned.

findings.title: Extension distributed via GitHub Releases + 'Load unpacked'
findings.description: The browser bridge extension is not published to the Chrome Web Store — users download a ZIP from GitHub Releases and load it as an unpacked extension. This skips Google's (limited) review process.
findings.exploit_scenario: A compromised release asset would install without store-level vetting. Mitigated by GitHub Release signatures + the fact that release artifacts are built inside the release.yml workflow.
findings.impact: Trust is anchored in the GitHub org (jackwener/opencli) and the release workflow. No independent third-party review.
findings.recommendation: Consider publishing to Chrome Web Store for defense-in-depth. Users should verify release source each update.
